Hey AD,

Let me express my views and go about with your different paragraphs.

On Twitter - You mention and believe that "Twitter is a breath of fresh air". To which I totally disagree. I would say its a tool, a new medium for information exchange. It could hold varied view which the mainstream media cannot encapsulate. That being said, it doesn't necessary mean that those varied view come in the open. I mean Who drives Twitter and tweets that trend? With their popularity - People from mainstream media and influential user. And the way it is designed and shaped recently - its more prominently a promotion tool. ( Promoted topics). And its no different from the mainstream media ( taking into account only the print media). You put forth your views on a certain topic and majority of  people without thinking or deliberating on it go with it. The more the cult - more the "meeeeh toooooh"

Modern Generation - Yeah I agree that its more of a "fab" to be modern and be open minded. And sadly individualism is lost in many cases. They portray these modern views when they have to comment on subject not concerning them but when it comes to implementation on their scope - they retrot double standards and hypocrisy. But I guess all is not lost if you keep looking for it - After all it takes people of all kinds to make this world. :)

The End - Totally agree on it. But I am not sure on the connotation of your word towards Anna Hazare. I am hoping it is what I feel and think it is then - I totally agree. Or else...

:-)

/2012/08/the-undesirability-of-truth.htm.message: Space missions have clearly defined objectives da. Each mission serves as a stepping stone to achieve clear cut medium and long term goals. India has an impressive record in indigenous space and nuclear research and we can't afford to lag behind in technological progress in these areas. They make many other things possible - estimating crop yield, anticipating droughts, assessing forest cover and providing effective communication and GPS facilities etc. Outcomes from each space mission are manifold. Grooming experts consistently in this field and scaling new heights is absolutely essential if India wants to be on the technological forefront. World scientists spending billions of dollars to see if there is 'a god particle' also is because of the reason that understanding these things would be almost revolutionary for technological studies and consequently boost human development (hopefully). It is 'the way of the future' (to quote Dicaprio from Aviator) :)

/2014/08/oiling-happiness.html.author: Adarsh

One of those times when you feel you can just link to another post and get the point across, but one has to try and write. I think my idea didn't get across properly. My whole blog is full of outrageous "what-ifs", and I like to think about them despite the logical impossibility of such a thing. I am wondering aloud if happiness is exhaustible like oil, and then I dismiss the idea myself (hopefully after planting it in a few minds). My chief problem is with artificial means to look for happiness. I am not aggregating happiness based on anything, but "scientific studies" are doing it. If companies insist on happiness of employees, there would be a lot of unfair discrimination. And I am,very uncomfortable with the idea that an employer will look to tinker with the natural mental state of its employees. Orwell was a visionary. Also, I feel that too much energy is spent looking for happiness. As you point out in your wonderful posts, there are many more important emotions which make us human. And no, I am not going to do or not-do anything based on such crazy ideas, and I am quite sure I don't have such an impact on anyone else too.

/2014/10/stop-shrug-and-fly-you-fools.ht.author: Guru
/2014/10/stop-shrug-and-fly-you-fools.ht.message: Very well written, but I disagree with certain points. "The hungry can then stare at Instagram photos of food to quench their hunger." Nope. Technology is highly disruptive and wakes up sleepy industries preventing them from slipping into lethargy. Technology cannot solve hunger for the penniless but can reduce the cost of production, transportation and distribution thereby driving down food prices. Technology can disrupt 200 year old industries which have evolved into monopolies without optimizing anything. That being said, technology does seem to be leaving a big mass of people behind, but that is precisely why pervasive internet connectivity can help. Every breakthrough technological advancement will leave a mass of people behind in that generation. When mobile phoneswere introduced, many people would have felt that it left behind a huge mass of population behind, but now small businesses owners(individual car shops, furtniture shops) etc use mobile phones to reach an audience they were unable to reach before. JustDial is another similar example of how technology can help the people with lower income trying to make a living. I can quote many such instances in India where technology has helped us reduce costs. The electricity board made online payments available which has cut down the cost of having to retain an employee or employees who was overburdened with bill-payments.

/2014/10/stop-shrug-and-fly-you-fools.ht.author: Adarsh
/2014/10/stop-shrug-and-fly-you-fools.ht.message: Thanks Guru! That's a well-thought out comment, and I will have to agree with you. I wouldn't deny the usefulness of technological advancements, starting from increasing life-expectancy to combating diseases. If at all I seem to be blaming technology, I got consciously carried away. My problem is with policy, and only proper policy can take technology to everyone. But no one seems to care, and there are more brains devoted to technology than to policy. It is as if we have given up on trying to solve such issues. Think of how many people are working at a smart-phone company thinking of ways to increase the resolution by a tiny bit? All for a premium clientele. And technology should theoretically narrow the gulf between the rich and the poor, but I fear that the gap might widen. A lot of it is to do with us, who can change things by changing priorities -- ours and hence that of many corporates.

/2014/10/stop-shrug-and-fly-you-fools.ht.author: Gopal Vijayaraghavan
/2014/10/stop-shrug-and-fly-you-fools.ht.message:
Really thought provoking.
Yes capitalism is predatory. It thrives on animal spirits. It has
led to great inequalities and concentration of wealth in a few hands.
Communism which was to be a force to take on capitalism fell into the
hands of dictators who discredited the philosophy of socialism. It left
the field open to capitalism. In the Indian context, a discretionary
patronage system resulted in the cornering of scarce natural resources by a few private
players. Now the judiciary is waking up
to its implications and stepped in. But
the role of Judiciary in such post facto actions after many years will also
have economic implications. Regulatory
system was slow to evolve and even when it took action, there were always some
stay orders by High Courts thwarting such action. But socialism had also certain drawbacks.
Public sector companies(with some notable exceptions) symbolised
inefficiency and as such could not take on the private sector in a liberalised
economy(Air India and BSNL are good illustrations). Trade union
leaders thrust outside from political parties promised sky and brought
down many well run companies since they
had no direct stake. It is a
dismal situation. And everybody carries on with the hope that
ultimately something good will come out. But the importance of Technology
in improving service delivery cannot be berated. It can definitely play a
positive role. A case in example
is the computerised railway reservation system. In a democracy there is always hope for
something better in future. And the
consolation is that we have the right to dissent if not become richer.

But I really feel that a lot of resources are spent on technologies we could do without. I am not sure if as many people are working to find a crue to Ebola as are working on making a microchip a wee-bit faster, or a mobile camera insignificantly more clear.

Hey Adarsh, nice choice of topic to write about! I'm sure you're penning down a lot of people's thoughts about such reactions.Thought I'd share two points that occurred to me.
You've mentioned that this post was to highlight the cases with irrational reactions. I'm with you on this one! I think it is created by the steeping hierarchy in our country. I haven't seen this is any other, at least not yet. It is so badly ingrained in our society, that it despises me. I know this is coming off as a really strong opinion, but it's an honest one.
About the obsession with flawlessness, I think it isn't the person or people that we end up having a problem with. It's with the service. We're in a society where consumer is king. With the vast variety available in every product, the consumer is left with tremendous choice, and promises are made about how buying a certain brand will give you certain (additional) benefits over another. So then why should the consumer not expect these things when he's paying for the service? I think it'd be lax to not point it out. Of course, this can be done well, without hurting people's feelings. And I don't think it's a person's imperfections that are being targetted in the process. It's in what's being created. So I think it's a two-way thing. I think it should be pointed out when a service is not able to provide what it says it will, but should be done without insulting people. And I think the person taking this feedback should not be taking it personally, but more objectively, as feedback for where the service can improve. Not sure if I've made myself clear, but I hope you got the point....
